entities.name: Amr ibn al-Jamuh
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ, a revered elder and chieftain of the Banu Salama clan in Medina, emerged as a poignant figure in early Islamic history, celebrated for his profound devotion and self-sacrifice despite a debilitating physical lameness. His life, culminating in martyrdom at the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, stands as a testament to the transformative power of faith within the nascent Muslim community. As one of the prominent Ansar companions of the Prophet Muhammad, Amr's narrative underscores the commitment of the Medinan converts who embraced Islam and offered crucial support during its formative years, even at great personal cost.

Prior to his conversion, Amr ibn al-Jamūḥ was a respected pagan leader, known for keeping an idol named Manāf, which his son Muʿādh ibn ʿAmr and other youths would surreptitiously desecrate, leading to his eventual acceptance of Islam. His most enduring contribution, however, arose from his fervent desire to participate in military campaigns despite his pronounced lameness. At the Battle of Uhud, his sons attempted to dissuade him, citing his disability, but Amr appealed directly to the Prophet Muhammad, expressing his desperate wish to fight and attain martyrdom, believing that God would grant him entry to Paradise. Muhammad, touched by his sincerity, granted him permission, and Amr fought valiantly, ultimately falling as a martyr alongside his son Khallād and his brother-in-law, a pivotal moment of sacrifice for the Muslim cause.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Amr ibn al-Jamuh's story provided a powerful and enduring model of faith, self-sacrifice, and the spiritual rewards of martyrdom within early Islam, inspiring countless Muslims across generations. His narrative contributed significantly to the moral and ethical framework of the nascent Muslim community.
